meta.title: Czech C1
meta.subtitle: 1,200 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Czech → English (see the Czech, recall the meaning) and English → Czech (see an English meaning, recall the Czech). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1,200 words and expressions for level C1 of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no Czech exam board publishes a word list beyond A2 — the A1 and A2 decks follow the official list of the permanent-residence exam, but the B1 citizenship exam and Charles University's CCE exams publish none. So 335 of the 1,200 words were written for Folio, a topic at a time, for the purposes the Common European Framework of Reference itself gives for C1 (the Council of Europe's level specifications stop at B2): demanding, longer texts and their implicit meaning, and language used flexibly for social, academic and professional purposes — the law and administration, economics and finance, politics and international relations, science, medicine and technology, the mind and society, philosophy and religion, history, literature, language and the arts, and the media and public debate, with the abstract nouns, verbs of nuance and connectives of a formal text — the next layer of vocabulary beyond A1 to B2 — together with the words of opinion and argument the level needs. They are Folio's choice, not an exam board's, and this is not an official word list. The other 865 are the commonest words of everyday Czech not already chosen, from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles, each word counted over all its forms. No word taught in A1, A2, B1 or B2 is repeated. The cards are ordered by that frequency, so the words met most often come first; the 13 multi-word expressions, which a list of single words cannot count, come last. Czech changes the endings of its nouns, adjectives and verbs, and stems change with them, so each card carries the forms that cannot be guessed, read from a dictionary rather than generated. 685 nouns show their gender, three cases of the singular and two of the plural. 206 verbs show their aspect and its partner, the forms for já (I), on (he) and oni (they) and the past of on — a perfective verb's present forms being its future. 8 adjectives show their comparative and superlative. Real example sentences come with 777 of the 1,200 words, three apiece for 390, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Meanings, forms and parts of speech: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency ordering: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
